author: Charles Babbage
title: The Ninth Bridgewater Treatise: A Fragment
side: No: an apparently new law shown by the engine was fixed in its original adjustment

author: Alfred Smee
title: The Mind of Man: Being a Natural System of Mental Philosophy
side: Partly: a machine can draw out consequences of what it is given, but its reach is narrow

author: Ambrose Bierce
title: Moxon's Master
side: Yes: a machine thinks, because matter absorbs the intelligence and purpose of its maker

author: Carl Friedrich Hindenburg
title: On Herr von Kempelen's Chess Player, with an Illustration and Description of his Speaking Machine
side: No: the automaton's fitting answers are prepared in advance and repeated

author: E. T. A. Hoffmann
title: Automata
side: Contested: Ferdinand takes the oracle's apt answers as evidence of a knowing mind; Ludwig says the questioner supplies the meaning

author: Charles-Georges Leroy
title: Philosophical Letters on the Intelligence and Perfectibility of Animals
side: No: a machine once set in motion acts always the same way; varying with circumstance shows reflection

author: Robert Willis
title: An Attempt to Analyse the Automaton Chess Player of Mr. de Kempelen
side: No: mechanism is limited and uniform and cannot meet unforeseen circumstances

author: George Henry Lewes
title: Problems of Life and Mind, Second Series: The Physical Basis of Mind
side: No: nothing we know of machines allows them to adjust to new circumstances

author: Morton Prince
title: The Nature of Mind and Human Automatism
side: Yes: nature has already built an automaton that adapts to unforeseen conditions

author: John Venn
title: Symbolic Logic (2nd ed.)
side: No: interpreting results takes tact and judgment, which a logic machine cannot supply

author: Henry Philip Tappan
title: The Doctrine of the Will, Determined by an Appeal to Consciousness
side: Yes: volition is a true first cause, and the body is the first mechanism it appropriates
review: weak: classifies causes; does not argue that volition moves the body

author: Charles Elam
title: Winds of Doctrine: Being an Examination of the Modern Theories of Automatism and Evolution
side: Yes: the felt causal power of volition is a fundamental intuition that automatism cannot overrule
review: weak: mocks the opposing view; states no reason of its own

author: Alexander Bain
title: Mind and Body: The Theories of Their Relation
side: Only as one side of a two-sided cause: mind-body causes mind-body

author: Morton Prince
title: The Nature of Mind and Human Automatism
side: Yes: consciousness is the brain process itself, so it causes action

author: Henry George Atkinson (with Harriet Martineau)
title: Letters on the Laws of Man's Nature and Development
side: Yes: all mental conditions are traced to physical causes; free will is a delusion

author: Moritz Wilhelm Drobisch
title: Moral Statistics and Human Freedom of the Will
side: No (on statistical grounds): regularities in crime and marriage rates do not show that individual acts are compelled
review: weak: rejects a statistical law of conduct but defers the free-will question

author: William B. Carpenter
title: The Doctrine of Human Automatism: A Lecture Delivered before the Sunday Lecture Society
side: No: the self can take in hand the formation of its own character

author: Charles Bray
title: The Philosophy of Necessity; or, The Law of Consequences, vol. 1
side: Yes, but only forward-looking: punishment is justified solely to prevent repetition

author: Daniel D. Whedon
title: The Freedom of the Will as a Basis of Human Responsibility and a Divine Government
side: No: a necessitated agent is as irresponsible as the springs of a gun-lock

author: Oliver Wendell Holmes
title: Mechanism in Thought and Morals
side: No: inherited tendencies belong to the machinery, for which the Creator alone is responsible

author: Henry Maudsley
title: Responsibility in Mental Disease
side: Partly: many sane people have lower responsibility because of their constitution

author: Thomas Rennell
title: Remarks on Scepticism, Especially as It Is Connected with the Subjects of Organization and Life
side: Yes: inert matter needs a principle of motion beyond its structure

author: William Lawrence
title: Lectures on Physiology, Zoology, and the Natural History of Man
side: No: a vital principle explains nothing and burdens physiology

author: Lionel S. Beale
title: Protoplasm; or, Matter and Life (3rd ed.)
side: Yes: life is a power distinct from ordinary force

author: H. Newell Martin
title: The Human Body: An Account of Its Structure and Activities and the Conditions of Its Healthy Working
side: No: the body is a self-building and self-repairing machine

author: Otto Bütschli
title: Mechanism and Vitalism
side: No: regeneration is restoration of equilibrium, like a water drop regaining its shape

author: J. Arthur Thomson
title: The System of Animate Nature (Gifford Lectures), vol. 1
side: Yes: continual self-repair marks living from inorganic change

author: Ralph Cudworth
title: The True Intellectual System of the Universe
side: No: the formation of an animal's organs cannot be explained by mechanism alone

author: Wilhelm His
title: Unsere Körperform und das physiologische Problem ihrer Entstehung
side: Yes: each stage of development from the egg should be derived as the necessary physical consequence of the stage before

author: Ronald Campbell Macfie
title: Heredity, Evolution, and Vitalism
side: No: organisms are not merely machines because the whole body is built up from the ovum

author: Antoine Arnauld and Pierre Nicole
title: Logic, or the Art of Thinking (Port-Royal Logic)
side: Partly: rules of reasoning can expose a bad argument, but most disagreement and error lies in judgments, not inferences

author: John Henry Newman
title: An Essay in Aid of a Grammar of Assent
side: No: reasoning about concrete matters is too multiform to be measured by rule

author: John Selden
title: Table-Talk
side: Yes: follow the law, because equity depends on the conscience of whoever is Chancellor

author: Francis Lieber
title: Legal and Political Hermeneutics
side: No: when circumstances change, the letter of a rule must give way to its intent

author: Eugen Ehrlich
title: Free Finding of Law and Free Legal Science
side: No: technical rule-application is a 'sin against the Holy Ghost'; justice depends on the judge's personality

author: Benjamin N. Cardozo
title: The Nature of the Judicial Process
side: Sometimes: judges may extend or restrict rules for social welfare, but certainty and uniformity are weighty parts of that welfare

author: Walter Allen Smith
title: Reform in the Government Service (Prize Essays on Civil Service Reform)
side: Yes, with limits: examinations are imperfect but better than patronage, and probation covers what they miss

author: W. Phillips (letter in Auberon Herbert's collection)
title: The Sacrifice of Education to Examination
side: No: a short conversation reveals fitness better than examinations with thousands of marks

author: Eugen Ehrlich
title: Free Finding of Law and Free Legal Science
side: No: passing examinations does not show fitness for the judge's office

author: Henry C. Link
title: Employment Psychology
side: No (for higher posts): tests cannot select executives because their work cannot be analysed or measured

author: Robert H. Thurston
title: A History of the Growth of the Steam-Engine
side: Yes: a great invention is a growth, not a creation of one mind
review: weak: invention as cumulative growth, not machines evolving

author: Otto Bütschli
title: Mechanism and Vitalism
side: Yes: machines develop by chance combinations from which the useful are kept, as organisms do under Darwin's theory

author: Gustav Wolff
title: Mechanism and Vitalism
side: No: machine development was steered throughout by conscious purpose, so it is not Darwinian

author: Peter Gaskell
title: The Manufacturing Population of England
side: Yes: as machines supply power and skill, workers become mere watchers and are displaced

author: Jean Grave
title: Machinery
side: No: machines harm workers only because masters own them; held in common they would serve everyone

author: Arthur Pound
title: The Iron Man in Industry
side: Partly: machines that absorb skill make the worker replaceable, but the subordination runs through the labour market

author: Christoph Wilhelm Hufeland
title: The Art of Prolonging Life
side: Qualified: prolong life only as active, purposeful life; mere longer existence is not the aim

author: William Sweetser
title: Human Life: Considered in its Present Condition and Future Developments, Especially with Reference to its Duration
side: Yes: inquiry into greatly prolonging life is legitimate; science has no forbidden fields

author: Harry Gaze
title: How to Live Forever: The Science and Practice
side: Yes: life should be perpetuated because one lifetime is too short for art and knowledge

author: C. A. Stephens
title: Natural Salvation: Immortal Life on the Earth from the Growth of Knowledge
side: Yes: science should aim at deathless life, which would be a higher kind of life

author: Joseph Butler
title: The Analogy of Religion (Part I, ch. 1, 'Of a Future Life')
side: Yes: limbs and sense organs are instruments, so replacing one with an artificial leg leaves the same living agent

author: Thomas Brown
title: Lectures on the Philosophy of the Human Mind
side: Qualified: personal identity includes the body, which may be totally replaced only if the change is gradual

author: Oliver Wendell Holmes
title: The Human Wheel, its Spokes and Felloes (in Soundings from the Atlantic)
side: Partly: a crude substitute marks and changes the person; a good artificial limb restores him
review: weak: describes a crude artificial leg; no claim about identity

author: Charles Knight (for the Society for the Diffusion of Useful Knowledge)
title: The Results of Machinery, Namely, Cheap Production and Increased Employment, Exhibited: Being an Address to the Working-Men of the United Kingdom
side: Yes: labor-saving tools are what keep working men from starvation

author: William Dodd
title: The Laboring Classes of England, Especially Those Engaged in Agriculture and Manufactures; in a Series of Letters
side: No: the spinner does five men's work for one man's wage and is worn out

author: Robert Dale Owen
title: Labor: Its History and Its Prospects. An Address Delivered before the Young Men's Mercantile Library Association of Cincinnati
side: No, not as now used: machines that should have freed the laborer compete with him

author: Frederick Perry Powers
title: Labor-Making Machinery: An Essay Read before the Chicago Philosophical Society, April 12, 1879
side: Yes: machinery shortens the working day and lightens toil

author: P. Gaskell
title: The Manufacturing Population of England: Its Moral, Social, and Physical Conditions, and the Changes Which Have Arisen from the Use of Steam Machinery
side: Diminish: the adult becomes a mere watcher needing no physical or intellectual exertion

author: Jean Grave
title: Le machinisme
side: Diminish: following a machine is learned in a week, so the trade is lost and the worker is replaceable

author: Émile Levasseur
title: Comparaison du travail à la main et du travail à la machine
side: Develop: machine work asks less of the body and more of the mind

author: James Hartness
title: The Human Factor in Works Management
side: Develop: repetition work builds concentration

author: American trade unions (statement of objections compiled by Robert F. Hoxie for the U.S. Commission on Industrial Relations)
title: Scientific Management and Labor, Appendix V: The Trade Union Objections to Scientific Management
side: Diminish: time study destroys craft skill and makes the worker a semi-automatic attachment to the machine

author: Arthur Pound
title: The Iron Man in Industry: An Outline of the Social Significance of Automatic Machinery
side: Both: skill is removed from most operatives and concentrated in a few designers

author: Jean Grave
title: Le machinisme
side: Everyone, through common ownership of the machines

author: Émile Levasseur
title: Comparaison du travail à la main et du travail à la machine
side: Mainly the consumer: neither worker nor employer caused the gain

author: William Preston Hill
title: Shadow or Substance: Socialism or Individualism?
side: Owners earn a return for risk, and in fact workers already receive most of the gain

author: Joseph John Gurney
title: Thoughts on Habit and Discipline
side: No: habit forms imperceptibly, and before we know it we have resigned our freedom

author: Paul Radestock
title: Habit and Its Importance in Education: An Essay in Pedagogical Psychology
side: Qualified no: extreme habituation robs a person of free self-determination, though mechanism saves effort

author: James Hartness
title: The Human Factor in Works Management
side: Yes: even habit imposed by routine leaves the mind free to wander
review: weak: describes routine habit; does not say it increases freedom

author: Armand Corre
title: Militarisme
side: Yes: military drill aims at automatism and the annihilation of character and will

author: Léon Furnémont
title: Le militarisme: voilà l'ennemi
side: Yes: passive, mechanical obedience kills intelligence and initiative

author: Charlotte Perkins Gilman
title: Concerning Children
side: Yes: the habit of obedience develops facility in following others, not judgment

author: Lucy Larcom
title: A New England Girlhood, Outlined from Memory
side: Strengthen: the mill bell's enforced regularity gave her order she could not have reached alone

author: LeBaron Russell Briggs
title: Routine and Ideals
side: Strengthen: routine imposed or self-imposed protects work from caprice

author: Christine Frederick
title: Household Engineering: Scientific Management in the Home
side: Strengthen: a schedule is not a treadmill; it is the only plan that forces regular rest

author: O. S. Fowler
title: Memory and Intellectual Improvement: Applied to Self-Education and Juvenile Instruction
side: Yes: those who keep accounts in their heads remember better than those who trust books

author: Eustace Miles
title: How to Remember, without Memory Systems or with Them
side: Partly: note-books properly relieve memory, but used in excess they take over work memory should do

author: O. S. Fowler
title: Memory and Intellectual Improvement: Applied to Self-Education and Juvenile Instruction
side: Yes: calculating mechanically instead of in the head causes the faculty's feebleness

author: George Trumbull Ladd
title: Psychology, Descriptive and Explanatory: A Treatise of the Phenomena, Laws, and Development of Human Mental Life
side: Yes: habitual use of an abacus turns calculation into association, not reasoning

author: William Cobbett
title: Cottage Economy
side: No, if the machine is the household's own: a hand- or horse-mill frees the farm from dependence on the distant mill
review: weak: recommends household mills; no claim about lost ability

author: Peter Gaskell
title: The Manufacturing Population of England
side: Yes: factory work leaves mill girls unable to run a household

author: Horace Bushnell
title: The Age of Homespun (discourse at the Litchfield County centennial, 1851), in Work and Play
side: Partly: more to gain than lose, but the old hardihood may go

author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
title: Works and Days, in Society and Solitude
side: Yes: each improvement to the engine unteaches its operator

author: Charlotte Perkins Gilman
title: Women and Economics
side: No: machinery took industry out of the home, and women followed it into paid work
review: weak: about women following industry to the mill, not lost self-provision

author: John Wilkins
title: Mercury: or the Secret and Swift Messenger (Conclusion)
side: No: an invention liable to abuse should still be published

author: Frederick Soddy
title: The Control of Wealth, in Science and Life: Aberdeen Addresses
side: No: the user, not the inventor, is responsible

author: Joseph Foster (testimony), in [Charles Knight]
title: The Results of Machinery (Working-Man's Companion)
side: No: machinery cannot and ought not to be stopped, even by those it harms

author: George Birdwood (quoted by A. K. Coomaraswamy)
title: The Industrial Arts of India (1880), quoted in The Indian Craftsman, Appendix II
side: Yes: machinery must be kept rigorously in its place

author: William Osler
title: Science and War
side: Yes: weapons whose cruelty is uncontrolled are tabooed by common consent
review: weak: about cruelty of a weapon, not uncontrollable consequences

author: Edward S. Farrow
title: Gas Warfare
side: No: gas should not be banned, since with masks it is humane
review: weak: defends gas as humane; restriction only implied

author: Arthur Pound
title: The Iron Man in Industry
side: No to opposing it; yes to controlling it

author: William Hamilton Drummond
title: The Rights of Animals, and Man's Obligation to Treat Them with Humanity
side: Yes: feeling, not the label "machine", grounds a claim to protection

author: Frances Power Cobbe
title: Zoophily, in The Peak in Darien
side: Yes: if they feel, they have claims, whatever the automatist says

author: William Ellery Channing
title: Slavery
side: No: a rational being belongs to itself, even though God made it

author: Francis Wayland
title: The Elements of Moral Science
side: Yes for God alone: creation gives the Creator unlimited possession, a relation beyond human analogy

author: Job Durfee
title: The Influence of Scientific Discovery and Invention on Social and Political Progress (Phi Beta Kappa oration)
side: Yes: invention continues the work of creation God began in Eden

author: Hollis Read
title: The Hand of God in History
side: Yes: steam, like printing, is a providential instrument for converting the world

author: Gerald Stanley Lee
title: The Voice of the Machines
side: Yes: engines express the creative spirit of God better than sermons

author: Moncure Daniel Conway
title: The Praying Machine, in Idols and Ideals
side: Yes: devotion handed to a mechanism becomes fetish and incantation

author: Okakura Kakuzo
title: The Awakening of Japan
side: Yes: the machine civilisation replaced superstition with an idolatrous worship of wealth

author: Gerald Stanley Lee
title: The Voice of the Machines
side: No: reverence for machines is the continuation of religion, not idolatry

author: [Charles Knight]
title: The Results of Machinery (Working-Man's Companion)
side: Yes: civilised society is marked by perfect instruments that save force

author: John Cordner
title: The Foundations of Nationality (sermon after the Grand Trunk Railway celebration, Montreal)
side: No: railways counted above people are Babylonian foundations

author: R. W. Church
title: Roman Civilisation, in The Gifts of Civilisation and Other Sermons and Lectures
side: No: railway and telegraph are not a test of civilisation

author: Rabindranath Tagore
title: Sadhana: The Realisation of Life
side: No: civilisation is judged by whether it treats man as spirit rather than machine

author: Khayr al-Din al-Tunisi
title: Réformes nécessaires aux États musulmans
side: Yes: Muslims may borrow what is good in worldly affairs without leaving their religion

author: Mahadev Govind Ranade
title: Present State of Indian Manufactures and Outlook of the Same (in Essays on Indian Economics)
side: No: importing machinery requires learning new civic habits

author: Lafcadio Hearn (Koizumi Yakumo)
title: Kokoro: Hints and Echoes of Japanese Inner Life
side: Yes, within limits: machinery worked only where it fit old aptitudes

author: G. Lowes Dickinson
title: Letters from John Chinaman (US title: Letters from a Chinese Official)
side: No: Western machinery brings Western disorders with it

author: Okakura Kakuzō
title: The Awakening of Japan
side: Yes: Japan took Western methods without changing its national character

author: Sun Yat-sen
title: The International Development of China
side: Yes: China can take the machinery and skip the Western path of competition

author: Katō Hiroyuki
title: Der Kampf ums Recht des Stärkeren und seine Entwickelung
side: Yes (descriptively): the stronger 'Kulturvölker' will rule; rights without strength are empty
review: weak: argues from strength, not technology

author: Gu Hongming (Ku Hung-ming)
title: Papers from a Viceroy's Yamen
side: No: machine-gun imperialism is vulgarity, not civilization

author: Romesh Chunder Dutt
title: The Economic History of India under Early British Rule
side: No: British railways served British trade, not India
review: weak: railways served British trade; no claim about the right to govern

author: John George Godard
title: Racial Supremacy: Being Studies in Imperialism
side: No: superior force gives no moral basis to rule

author: Okakura Kakuzō
title: The Book of Tea
side: No: military success is no claim to civilization

author: Edmund Burke
title: Reflections on the Revolution in France
side: No: the state is a contrivance, but redesign is not a matter of a priori theory

author: Johann Caspar Bluntschli
title: The Theory of the State
side: No: the state is an organism, not a dead machine

author: Woodrow Wilson
title: Constitutional Government in the United States
side: No: government is a living thing, not a machine

author: Henry Taylor
title: The Statesman
side: No: a statesman needs a strong conscience, scaled to public consequences
review: weak: statesman's conscience, not officials carrying out rules

author: Johann Caspar Bluntschli
title: The Theory of the State
side: Mostly yes: obey after remonstrance, except where the order is a crime or against morality

author: Nitobe Inazō
title: Bushido, the Soul of Japan
side: No: a retainer must not make his conscience the slave of his lord

author: Hermann Lotze
title: Microcosmus: An Essay Concerning Man and his Relation to the World
side: No, but felt as yes: sensation at the tool's tip is a useful illusion

author: Oliver Wendell Holmes Sr.
title: The Human Wheel, its Spokes and Felloes (in Soundings from the Atlantic)
side: Yes, through practice: the wooden limb comes to be inhabited

author: J. A. Etzler
title: The Paradise within the Reach of All Men, without Labour, by Powers of Nature and Machinery
side: Yes: machinery puts at our disposal powers millions of times our own

author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
title: Works and Days (in Society and Solitude)
side: No: the machine unmakes and unteaches its operator

author: Lafcadio Hearn (Koizumi Yakumo)
title: Kokoro: Hints and Echoes of Japanese Inner Life
side: No: dependence on machinery numbs native power

author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
title: Feathertop: A Moralized Legend (in Mosses from an Old Manse)
side: No: the love ends when the artificial nature is seen

author: Thomas Hardy
title: Barbara of the House of Grebe (in A Group of Noble Dames)
side: Yes, while the image stays perfect

author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
title: Monsieur du Miroir (in Mosses from an Old Manse)
side: Yes, partly: counterfeit sympathy is better than none
review: weak: a mirror image, not an artificial companion (analogue)

author: Victor Hugo
title: Les Misérables (Part II, 'Cosette')
side: Yes for a child: imagining that something is somebody meets a real need
review: weak: a child's doll, not an artificial companion (analogue)
